$comment: Who says which words in this chapter (docs/voice-narration-plan.md section 3). Drafted by `npm run voice:script`; a line with no entry is read by the narrator. A person checks each draft and sets `reviewed` to true; re-drafting only touches missing and stale entries.

lines.text: The lead drover from the ford spots you.
"Mudlarks! Up you get!"
he booms. It is what he calls everybody he likes. You ride the tailboard with your legs dangling, eating dried apples.
A prospector called Ma Ruddle watches her wagon being auctioned.
"Never mind the wagon. I've lost my nephew Tib! Small. Orange hat. Talks to horses."
Find him, and she will give you her depot papers.
Your kitsune climbs onto a crate and booms,
"LOST! ONE SMALL BOY! ORANGE HAT! TALKS TO HORSES!"
The whole lane stops to listen. Then forty people point the same way.
Ma Ruddle can't shout over the auction. A centaur relay runner skids up.
"Small boy, orange hat, talks to horses? Hand me the word. I'll pass it down the line."
"Small orange horse,"
says one runner, and gallops off. Luckily the next runner has met Tib. Word comes back: found!
There! An orange hat bobs above the crowd, then ducks behind one of three wagons.
"Watch which one he hides behind,"
says Ma Ruddle, wringing her hands.
There is Tib, chatting with a pony. Ma Ruddle hugs him, then gives you a honeycake and a folded bill of sale.
"For the stone I left at the depot,"
she says.
"I'm going home. You have it."
By the road, helpers in dark robes serve soup in big tents. Little crystals hum on strings around their necks. A ladler named Wend waves you in.
"Kindness first,"
says Wend.
Beside the lane, people in dark robes have put up rest tents, with DEEP HOLLOW stitched small on the flaps. Behind the soup pot is Wend from the ford.
"You made it across!"
says Wend, and says each of your names without being told.
"The world's a little broken, isn't it?"
says Wend.
"Wrong-colored sky, humming stones. We could fix it, right at the root. Will you carry a letter north for us?"
Wend's crystal hums the stones' note. By the pot sits a coin box.
"Maybe,"
you say. Wend nods as if maybe means yes, and slips a sealed letter into your pack,
"in case."
All day you feel it in there, like a stone in a boot.
"No, thank you,"
you say, kindly and clearly. Wend smiles just as warmly, which is somehow the strangest part.
"Kindness first anyway,"
says Wend, tucking a warm roll into your pack. The crystal keeps humming.
You carry posts until your arms feel like noodles, and you plant every one straight. The road boss looks down the new curve and nods.
"Good work. The relay will sing about this,"
she says, and she does not sound like she is joking.
"Nothing will pass the hollow where the stone fell,"
says the road boss. She walks you along the detour: old bridge, pond, depot barn. Remember that order. It will get you past the silly signs ahead.
You hold the tuned charm over the hollow. It sings, faint and thin, though the stone was carried off weeks ago. The ground remembers.
"Well,"
says the road boss.
"That explains a thing or two."
A Skywarden patrol has stopped the road. Sergeant Holloway wants a toll of two coins, for Redspire, the wardens' citadel.
"Only arithmetic,"
he says. He also has a form marked WORKS INSTEAD, with its own box.
Your griffin and the sergeant swap sky news like old flyers: wind at the bridge, ash over the mountain, a storm sitting on the sea. Holloway writes it all down.
"Useful,"
he says, and waves you through.
You pay. Sergeant Holloway writes PAID, POLITE in his ledger and hands you a receipt, then a receipt for the receipt.
"Arithmetic,"
he says, almost kindly.
"The only thing up here that isn't shouting."
Clerk Pennywhistle runs a depot barn full of strongboxes. Number nine rings like a dinner bell. That stone can be claimed, with the right paper.
"There is a form for deciding which form,"
the clerk says happily.
Pennywhistle opens strongbox nine.
"The Depot Stone. Claimed."
He writes your names and hands over the ringing gem.
"Keep it away from my pens."
Behind him, strongbox ten gives a loud thump.
At the noon stop, a ring of travelers is swapping news, and the news has clearly been swapped a great many times.
"On the River Road,"
says one,
"a troll charges you a story instead of a coin."
"On the Wild Road,"
says another,
"the marsh steals your boots and gives back different boots."
Everybody turns to you.
"What's your news?"
A dragonling courier trots down from the north on a pony, ringing ding, ding, pause, ding.
"Boundary news! It must reach the river,"
she pants. She looks very tired.
Ding, ding, pause, ding. You get it exactly right, and far away to the south, very faintly, another bell rings it back. The courier beams.
"You'd make a grandmother one day,"
she says, which is the biggest compliment she knows.
Ding, pause, ding, ding, ding. The courier goes pink.
"That one means the cake is ready,"
she whispers. Far to the south, a whole camp sits down hopefully to wait for cake. She takes the bell back, giggling, and rings it properly.
"The grandmothers are turning back pry bars at the boundary stones,"
says the courier.
"Whole wagons of them. Not spoons. Spoons are fine."
Her pony nudges you for attention.
You ring the answer every dragonling child knows: heard you, coming home. The courier's mouth falls open.
"You're from the hills! The grandmothers will want YOU."
She rings the news of you down the road, proud as anything.
At the relay campfire, centaurs sing one verse for each landmark. New detours mean new verses.
"Your turn, travelers,"
hums a centaur called Old Corran. He wants your verse for the road.
Sergeant Holloway is already behind the Skywarden supply wagon.
"Third ash wind this week,"
he says, writing BUSY under MOUNTAIN. He offers you a cracker. It is extremely dry.
The road boss holds a rope while you guide the last post into its hole.
"The relay will find that in the dark,"
she says, and gives you a jar of glowing moss for the night.
Past the sergeant's table, a striped pole swings up and down. A patrol goat chews a ledger page.
"Cross on the lift,"
says Holloway, writing GOAT, HUNGRY.
Strongbox ten grows three legs and starts eating a ledger. Eleven tries to follow.
"Mire mimics!"
cries Pennywhistle.
"Ten has been empty since spring!"
Drive them out before they eat the stamps.
The mimics slink off, disguised as rocks. Pennywhistle thanks you with a brass whistle from lost property.
"Lost since spring,"
he says.
"So is my patience."
While the courier gulps water, her chubby pony nudges your elbow. Her name is Dumpling, and she is hot, itchy and sulky.
"She wants a fuss,"
says the courier.
"Any fuss will do."
Old Corran taps the new verses one landmark at a time, and each glows in the firelight.
"Now tap them back in road order,"
he says.
You tap it back note for note.
"There,"
says Old Corran.
"The road just learned you."
Old Corran taps the first landmark with you.
"The road just learned you."
Every post lands right.
"My crew will help if the ash wind catches you,"
says the road boss.
The courier rings ding, ding, pause, ding. Watch, then echo it.
"Don't skip the pause,"
she pants,
"or people start looking for cake."
Ding, pause, ding, ding, ding.
"That means the cake is ready,"
she whispers. Far south, a camp waits for cake.
Every gem hums the same note, you tell them. An old woman nods.
"Noticed that,"
she says. A nearby wagon hums as if voting.
